newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia says steel privatisation deal signed soon.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia says steel privatisation deal signed soon.

text.p: A prolonged deal to privatise Malaysia's ailing Perwaja Steel will be signed soon, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Monday.
Lion Corp Bhd, one of the two steelmakers invited to rescue Perwaja, should be ready to come on board, Mahathir said.
"They never withdrew," Mahathir told reporters after launching Perwaja's new 700,000-tonnes a year capacity beam and section mill in northern Kedah state.
"They expressed interest, but they were negotiating the terms. I hope they come in," he said.
Mahathir said the government was close to finalising the privatisation programme with the interested groups. An aide said it could be signed as early as this week.

"Maju Holdings (Sdn Bhd) will be the major shareholder with 51 percent, Lion Group will take 30 percent, the government of Trengganu (state) will take five percent and the balance will be with the federal government," he said. Trengganu state lies on the eastern coast of the Malay Peninsula.
The government announced on January 2 that it was assuming nearly 2.9 billion ringgit ($1.16 billion) in losses racked up by Perwaja.

Last year, Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim disclosed to parliament the financial troubles of the Japanese-designed steel plant aimed at being the centrepiece of the country's heavy industrialisation programme.
The Anti-Corruption Agency is investigating irregularities in the company, whose managing director Eric Chia resigned in August 1995.
"Perwaja's future is promising because this time we are starting on a clean slate," Mahathir said.
He declined to say what the new shareholders were paying for Perwaja's equity.
The government had earlier estimated they would have to inject about one billion ringgit to revive Perwaja.

Abu Shahid Mohamed, executive chairman of Maju Holdings and chairman of Perwaja's executive managing committee, told reporters the government's responsibility for the steel firm's losses would be less than two billion ringgit after the new owners paid for their shares.
Maju Holdings has said it expects the steel maker to turn a net profit of 100 million ringgit by 1998.
Lion Group Chairman William Cheng said in December the level of funding required from the major shareholders to revive the debt-saddled company was the major problem.
"We ourselves are having quite huge expansion plans since the last five to six months to strengthen our steel division," he said after the group's annual meeting.

Mahathir said in a speech earlier the country remained committed to having a strong steel industry to avoid importing its steel requirements. A strong steel industry was often used as a barometer of economic progress, he added.
